Lunar Landing. The successful descent of a spacecraft to the Moon's surface—one of humanity's most ambitious engineering achievements. The first manned landing occurred on July twentieth, 1969, when Apollo 11 touched down in the Sea of Tranquility, fundamentally transforming both space exploration and human self-understanding. These missions required unprecedented precision in navigation, propulsion, and life-support systems to overcome the Moon's harsh environment.

The Moon's low gravity—one-sixth of Earth's—and lack of atmosphere simplify landing in some ways but require specialized hardware for power, guidance, and safe descent rates. Apollo 11's lunar module, piloted by Neil Armstrong, executed a manual landing with only seconds of fuel remaining after computer guidance initially targeted a boulder-strewn crater.

The Lunar Module used throttleable descent engines and a two-stage design, with an ascent stage to return the crew to orbit and rendezvous with the command module. Lunar landings required retrograde burns to shed velocity and enter a powered descent, solving the problem of landing without an atmosphere to use for braking. The Apollo missions used a two-stage lunar approach: the command module remained in orbit while the lunar module descended, then ascended to dock for the return to Earth.

Landing sites were chosen to be relatively flat with good lighting, avoiding steep terrain and deep craters that could tip the fragile spacecraft. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, collecting 842 pounds of samples that revolutionized planetary geology. The lunar module's descent stage remained on the Moon as an abandoned base, while the ascent stage fired to meet the orbiting command module.

Deployment of experiments included seismic instruments and a laser retroreflector that allowed precise Earth-Moon distance measurements for decades. Landing on the Moon required solving the problem of dust adhesion, as lunar regolith clung to spacesuits and equipment, threatening seals and mechanisms.

Apollo 11 achieved the first manned lunar landing, and Apollo 13 was the crisis mission that tested the redundancy and ingenuity of both spacecraft and ground teams. The Space Race was the Cold War competition that drove the urgency and funding for lunar exploration. Neil Armstrong was the mission commander and first person to walk on the Moon. Buzz Aldrin was the lunar module pilot who joined Armstrong on the surface. The Moon itself is Earth's only natural satellite and a geologically diverse world. NASA is the agency that designed, built, and managed the Apollo program.
